function: Parametric near-field channel estimation (azimuth, elevation, distance) by deep-unfolded maximum likelihood with a CNN denoiser, then joint hybrid and RIS passive beamforming for sum rate (pp. 1, 3).
system: BS ULA N=8 with hybrid beamforming, passive reflecting RIS UPA M=128, K=5 single-antenna users, direct link neglected; mmWave/THz band, no carrier frequency given (pp. 3, 9).
method: Deep unfolding of gradient-descent ML estimation (MLADU) and hybrid beamforming (HBADU) with trainable step sizes, plus CNN residual denoiser; Adam, label-free losses (received signal, sum rate), unsupervised (pp. 5-8).
data_channel: Custom simulation: BS-RIS far-field Saleh-Valenzuela LoS, RIS-user spherical-wave near-field LoS (L1=L2=1); users random in a 5 m-radius cylinder around the RIS; no dataset or measurement (pp. 4, 9).
test_conditions: Single simulated setup (N=8, M=128, K=5, 30 pilots); sweeps of SNR, pilots (10-50) and RIS elements (64-224); no separate training and test conditions stated (pp. 9-10).
baselines: Non-learned: LS, gradient-descent ML (MLGD), CRB, random RIS, gradient-descent hybrid beamforming (HBAGD). Own variants: MLADU without denoiser, fully digital beamforming. No earlier learned method (pp. 9-10).
metrics: NMSE of the near-field channel (Eq. 46), gap of NMSE to the Cramer-Rao bound, sum rate of users, convergence of loss L4 versus epochs (pp. 9-11).
complexity: Order O(VJS(4K+M^2)) for MLADU versus O(TJS(4K+M^2)) for gradient-descent ML; HBADU O(KJS(qK+M^2+N N_RF+K N_RF)); no runtime or parameter count (p. 9).
q1_support: p. 4: "Based on the Saleh-Valenzuela (SV) channel model, Gbs can be written as"; Eq. (4) builds the RIS-user near-field LoS path by hand and p. 9 places users at random around the RIS. Custom simulator: no 3GPP TR 38.901, QuaDRiGa, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured data is used.
q2_support: p. 9: "the number of pilot symbols is set to 30" in one setup (N = 8, M = 128, K = 5); pp. 10-11 sweep SNR, pilots and RIS size without saying that training used other conditions. p. 7 only claims "MLADU has strong generalization ability" and shows no test in a new scenario.
q3_support: p. 9: "The denoising network is not considered in this scheme compared with the MLADU scheme." This is an ablation of the proposed method. The other baselines are LS, MLGD, CRB (p. 9), random RIS and HBAGD (p. 10), all non-learned; no earlier learned estimator or beamformer, and no standard DNN or CNN applied to the problem, is compared.
q4_support: p. 9: "It can be see that the complexity of MLADU is lower than that of the ML algorithm based on GD." The section gives O(VJS(4K+M^2)) for MLADU and O(KJS(qK+M^2+N N_RF+K N_RF)) for HBADU.
q5_support: p. 9: "The coordinates of the user equipment are randomly generated within a cylindrical region centered on the RIS"; channels are simulated and the paper gives no link or DOI for code or data and uses no public or measured dataset.
notes: Area 2 versus 3: the method solves two functions of areas 1 to 3 jointly (JNCEBD, p. 3: "joint network of channel estimation and beamforming design (JNCEBD) to maximize the sum rate (SR) of users"). Area 2 was chosen because the title, most of the abstract (p. 1) and the first novelty are the parametric channel estimation, evaluated with NMSE against the CRB (Figs. 5-6, p. 10); the beamforming stage reports the sum rate (Figs. 8-9, pp. 10-11), so area 3 is the alternative if the reviewer judges the sum rate to be the main metric. Training is done inside the Adam-updated iterations of Algorithms 1 and 2 (pp. 7, 9); the paper never states a train/test split, hence q2 = 0. Perfect CSI is assumed in the beamforming stage (footnote 2, p. 8). The text says V layers but p. 9 sets "the number of layers as K = 8" (typo in the paper).
